title: Michel Foucault

cards.b: Michel Foucault (1926-84) changed how we think about power, knowledge and the self. Where liberals and Marxists look for power in the state or in class, he finds it in clinics, prisons, schools and everyday habits. Questions on power (Paper I) increasingly bring him in.

Early works study how knowledge forms: Madness and Civilization (1961), The Birth of the Clinic (1963), The Order of Things (1966). Method called archaeology digs for the rules that make some statements possible in an age.

Later he used genealogy (after Nietzsche): tracing how present practices came out of contingent, often brutal, histories. Discipline and Punish (1975) and The History of Sexuality (vol. 1, 1976) are the key genealogies.

Power and knowledge imply each other. Experts, such as doctors, psychiatrists and criminologists, produce 'truth' about people, and this truth lets institutions control them. 'Truth' is a product of discourse, the system of statements and practices that decides what is sayable and normal.

Power is not only a 'no' (repression). It is productive: it makes subjects, norms and desires.

In Discipline and Punish Foucault shows the shift from public torture (Damiens, 1757) to the prison. Modern power works through surveillance, normalising judgement and examination. He takes Bentham's Panopticon as the model: the inmate, never sure when watched, polices himself. Armies, schools, factories and hospitals produce 'docile bodies'.

From the late 1970s: biopower manages life itself, through births, health, sexuality and population statistics. In History of Sexuality he argues that Victorian 'repression' of sex actually produced endless talk of sex and new identities. Governmentality (lectures 1977-79) covers the art of governing populations through knowledge, economy and security, including neoliberal rule.

'Where there is power, there is resistance.' Resistance is local and plural, not one grand revolution. Late Foucault studied technologies of the self: how people shape themselves through ethical practice. He supported prison, gay and Iranian-revolution causes, which drew criticism.

Keep the name, the year and the one-line claim ready. These three details are what examiners look for when they check a concept.

• Habermas: no normative ground to say why power is bad.
  • Marxists: ignores class and the economy and the state.
  • Feminists (Fraser): helpful on bodies but blind to gender; others (Butler) build on him.
  • Charges of relativism and weak historical evidence.

In an answer, give two points for and two against, then close with a balanced verdict. Examiners reward a clear stand backed by a named thinker or case.

Foucaultian ideas appear in the study of colonial knowledge (census, caste classification, Bernard Cohn), the surveillance debate around Aadhaar and the right to privacy (Puttaswamy, 2017), and the reading-down of Section 377 (Navtej Johar, 2018). The Subaltern Studies school drew on him. Gandhi's critique of modern prisons, medicine and courts in Hind Swaraj (1909) is an early parallel.

"Explain Foucault's concept of power/knowledge."
"How does Foucault's idea of power differ from the Marxist and liberal views?"
"What is the Panopticon and why does Foucault use it?"

Structure: concept, method, power/knowledge, discipline, biopower, resistance, critique, India.

Marks tip: open with a one-line definition, use two or three named thinkers, cases or Articles, add one Indian example, and end with a balanced, forward-looking line. Keep within the word limit.
